_meta.descricao: The Ten Commandments commented on one by one, with biblical references, and the five precepts of the Church.
_meta.aviso: Introductory catechetical explanation of each commandment; concrete and complex moral cases always require the guidance of a confessor or spiritual director, not merely the reading of this summary.
_meta.revisao_editorial: The numbering and exact division of the Ten Commandments vary slightly among Christian traditions (the Catholic and Lutheran traditions, following Saint Augustine, divide them differently from the Jewish and Reformed traditions); this collection follows the traditional Catholic division, also used by the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
fontes_gerais: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section Two ("The Ten Commandments")

itens.titulo: "You shall love God above all things"
itens.resumo: The first commandment forbids idolatry and requires worshiping God alone, the foundation of the whole Law.
itens.corpo: "You shall have no other gods before me" (Ex 20:3) is the foundation of the whole Decalogue: to recognize and worship the one true God, refusing every form of idolatry — not only the worship of stone idols, but also the modern idolatries of money, power, pleasure, or the self, when they are placed in the position that belongs to God alone. It includes the sins of superstition, divination, magic, and voluntary atheism.

itens.titulo: "You shall not take the name of God in vain"
itens.resumo: The second commandment requires respect for the holy name of the Lord and forbids blasphemy, perjury, frivolous oaths, and the magical use of the divine name.
itens.corpo:
"You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Ex 20:7) commands respect for the name of the Lord and regulates the use of speech in holy things, depending, like the first commandment, on the virtue of religion (CCC 2142). The Catechism's entry places the commandment in the light of Mt 5:33-34 — "Do not swear at all" — showing that the Gospel's demand goes beyond the mere prohibition of false oaths. The name of God is not an anonymous force: it reveals the divine essence. To Moses God revealed himself as "I AM WHO I AM" (Ex 3:13-15; cf. CCC 213), a name that Israel, out of reverence, ceased to pronounce, replacing it with the title "Lord" (Adonai in Hebrew, Kyrios in Greek; cf. CCC 209). The Catechism also recalls other Old Testament names — Elohim, a plural of fullness, and El-Shaddai, "the Almighty."

The doctrine distinguishes three principal offenses. Blasphemy consists in uttering against God, inwardly or outwardly, words of hatred, reproach, or defiance, and is in itself a grave sin (CCC 2148); it is also blasphemous to invoke the name of God to justify criminal practices, to reduce peoples to slavery, or to torture or put to death. Perjury is calling on God as witness to a lie, a grave offense against the second commandment (CCC 2163). Oaths and swearing made lightly, without the intention of blaspheming, are nonetheless a lack of respect toward the Lord (CCC 2149).

The commandment "also forbids the magical use of the divine name" (CCC 2149), condemning every attempt to manipulate God's power through superstitious formulas. On the other hand, it does not forbid every oath. Saint Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (II-II, q. 89, a. 2), sets out the classical doctrine: an oath is lawful when three conditions are met — truth (not asserting what is false), justice (not corroborating what is unlawful), and necessity with discretion, that is, not swearing lightly. Saint Jerome, commenting on Mt 5:34, observed that the Savior did not forbid swearing by God, but swearing by creatures (heaven, earth, Jerusalem, one's own head). The Catechism confirms that the holiness of God's name requires that one not have recourse to it for frivolous matters, and that one may refuse an oath demanded by an illegitimate authority or for purposes contrary to the dignity of persons (CCC 2155).

The respect owed to the name of God extends to the names of Jesus Christ, of the Virgin Mary, and of the saints, and to sacred realities, above all the Eucharist (CCC 2146). The summary of the Catechism sums up the commandment in three points: the name of the Lord is holy; the improper use of this name is forbidden; and a false oath, which calls on God as witness to a lie, is a grave offense (CCC 2160-2163). At the same time, the faithful are called to positive witness: to confess and invoke the name of the Lord with reverence, to bless it and to glorify it (CCC 2143).

Saint Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 89, a. 2 (on the lawfulness of oaths)
Saint Jerome, Commentary on Matthew (on Mt 5:34)

itens.titulo: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy"
itens.resumo: The third commandment asks for the sanctification of Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, through participation in Mass and rest from work.
itens.corpo: In the Old Testament, the precept referred to the Sabbath, the memorial of God's rest after creation (Gen 2:2-3). For Christians, the precept was transferred to Sunday, the "Lord's Day," in memory of the Resurrection of Christ. The Church asks for participation in Sunday Mass and abstention from work and activities that hinder the worship owed to God and the proper rest of soul and body.

itens.resumo: The fourth commandment asks for the respect and obedience owed to parents in childhood, and for mutual support between parents and children throughout life.
itens.corpo: "Honor your father and your mother" (Ex 20:12) is the only one of the Ten Commandments accompanied by a promise: "that your days may be long." It governs the relationship between parents and children — obedience and respect in childhood, material and spiritual care and support for parents in old age — and the Catholic tradition extends its principle to all relations of legitimate authority in society.

itens.resumo: The fifth commandment protects the inviolability of human life, from its natural beginning to its natural end.
itens.corpo: "You shall not kill" (Ex 20:13) is the foundation of Catholic teaching on the inviolability of human life from conception until natural death, and the basis of the Church's opposition to direct abortion and euthanasia. It also includes the prohibition of suicide, of mistreatment, and of everything that unnecessarily endangers one's own health and life or those of others, while recognizing the right to legitimate defense.

itens.resumo: The Sixth Commandment calls to chastity in every state of life and protects the fidelity and unity of marriage.
itens.corpo: "You shall not commit adultery" (Ex 20:14) is the foundation of the teaching on chastity — a virtue that successfully integrates sexuality within the person, proper to each state of life — and on conjugal fidelity. The Catholic moral tradition treats all of sexual morality under this commandment: besides adultery, also fornication, masturbation, pornography, and prostitution, always starting from the positive principle that human sexuality is called to be fully realized in the total and fruitful self-giving of marriage.

itens.resumo: The seventh commandment protects the right to property and demands justice in economic relations.
itens.corpo: "You shall not steal" (Ex 20:15) protects the legitimate right to private property and justice in economic relations, forbidding theft in any form — including commercial fraud, tax evasion, corruption, and deliberate damage to the property of others or to public property. At the same time, Catholic tradition reminds us that private property carries a "social mortgage": the goods of the earth are originally destined for all.

itens.resumo: The eighth commandment requires truth in words and forbids lying, calumny, detraction, and false witness.
itens.corpo: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor" (Ex 20:16) establishes the duty to tell the truth and to respect the honor and reputation of others. It forbids false witness in court, lying, calumny (falsely attributing a fault to someone), detraction (revealing without a legitimate reason the real faults of another), and flattery motivated by self-interest.

itens.titulo: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife"
itens.resumo: The ninth commandment calls for the purification of the heart and of desires, beyond external conduct.
itens.corpo: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife" (Ex 20:17) shifts the focus of morality from the external act to interior desire, completing the sixth commandment: it asks not only for fidelity in actions, but for the purification of the heart itself and of thoughts, recognizing that disordered desire, even when not carried out, already compromises interior purity.

itens.titulo: "You shall not covet your neighbor's goods"
itens.resumo: The tenth commandment completes the seventh on the level of interior desire: it forbids coveting the goods of others, avarice, and envy, and calls for poverty of heart.
itens.corpo:
"You shall not covet [...] anything that is [your neighbor's]" (Ex 20:17) unfolds and completes the ninth commandment: while the latter forbids concupiscence of the flesh, the tenth has as its object the coveting of the goods of others (CCC 2514; 2534). The biblical text appears in two versions — Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21 — with differences of order and vocabulary that Tradition has read without contradiction: in Exodus it opens with the house, in Deuteronomy with the wife. The Catechism situates this commandment at the root: the Law here reaches the intention of the heart, according to the word of Christ, "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mt 6:21).

The Catechism distinguishes two condemned interior dispositions. The first is greed, the desire for immoderate appropriation of earthly goods, born of the immoderate passion for riches and their power (CCC 2536), the root of the theft, robbery, and fraud forbidden by the seventh commandment. The second is envy — "sadness at the sight of another's goods and the immoderate desire to acquire them for oneself" (CCC 2553), listed among the capital sins. The Catechism illustrates it with the parable told by the prophet Nathan to David, of the poor man who had only one ewe lamb, and recalls that "through the devil's envy death entered the world" (Wis 2:24). Saint Gregory the Great, cited in this context, identified envy as the source of hatred.

It should be noted that the commandment does not condemn desire itself, but disordered desire. The sensitive appetite to eat when hungry or to warm oneself when cold is good in itself; it becomes sinful when it does not respect the limits of reason and leads one to unjustly covet what is not ours (CCC 2535). The catechetical tradition therefore relates the tenth commandment to the seventh Beatitude and to the struggle for "poverty of heart": all the faithful are called to order their affections rightly, so that the use of earthly things and attachment to riches do not hinder progress in charity (CCC 2545). Jesus gave the example in the poor widow of Jerusalem, who out of her poverty put in all she had to live on (Lk 21:4), and warned that the precept of detachment from riches is a condition for entering the Kingdom of heaven (CCC 2544).

The commandment, therefore, is not merely a rule about property, but a spiritual program: it forbids letting oneself be dominated by the lust of the eyes, which leads to violence and injustice, and teaches that the baptized overcome envy through goodwill, humility, and abandonment to divine providence (CCC 2554). The summary of the Catechism formulates it as a path: "Detachment from riches is necessary for entering the Kingdom of heaven" (CCC 2556).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church §§ 2534-2557 (official text, vatican.va)

itens.titulo: Attending Mass on Sundays and Holy Days of Obligation
itens.resumo: First precept of the Church: to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, and to abstain from unnecessary work.
itens.corpo: The first precept of the Church obliges the faithful to participate in Mass on Sundays and on the established holy days of obligation, and to abstain from work and activities that prevent the sanctification of these days. It is not an arbitrary addition to the third commandment: it is its institutional concretization, ensuring that the Christian community actually gathers regularly to celebrate the paschal mystery.

itens.titulo: Confess your grave sins at least once a year
itens.resumo: The second precept of the Church: to seek the sacrament of Reconciliation at least annually when there is grave sin.
itens.corpo: The second precept establishes the indispensable minimum of sacramental life: whoever is aware of grave sin must confess at least once a year, thus preparing to receive the Eucharist worthily. It does not prevent, and the Church recommends, much more frequent confession as an ordinary means of spiritual growth.

itens.titulo: Receive Communion at Least at Easter
itens.resumo: Third precept of the Church: to receive the Eucharist at least once a year, during the Easter season, joining the faithful to the center of the liturgy.
itens.corpo:
The third precept sets the minimum of Eucharistic participation. The Catechism formulates it thus: "You shall receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at least during the Easter season", guaranteeing "at the very least" the reception of the Body and Blood of the Lord "in connection with the Paschal feast, the origin and center of the Christian liturgy" (CCC 2042). The Code of Canon Law gives it juridical form in canon 920 §1: "After being initiated into the Most Holy Eucharist, each of the faithful is obliged to receive holy communion at least once a year". Canon 920 §2 specifies the time and the exceptions: the precept "must be fulfilled during the Easter season unless it is fulfilled for a just cause at another time during the year".

The "Easter season" here is not to be confused with Lent, nor does it extend beyond Pentecost as an ordinary deadline: liturgically, it is the period of fifty days that runs from Easter Sunday, the Sunday of the Resurrection, to Pentecost Sunday, which the Church celebrates "as one great feast day" (cf. CCC 2042 and canon 920, which speaks of the "Easter season"). Paschal communion is thus tied to the summit of the liturgical year, and not to an isolated date. The faithful who are prevented by a just cause may fulfill the precept at another time of the year.

The precept is associated, in practice, with the duty of annual confession, the second precept of the Church (canon 989: every member of the faithful who has reached the age of discretion is obliged to confess serious sins at least once a year). The Catechism explains that this second precept "ensures preparation for the Eucharist by the reception of the sacrament of Reconciliation" (CCC 2042). The connection between Easter confession and communion goes back to the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), convoked and presided over by Pope Innocent III, whose canon 21, "Omnis utriusque sexus", ordered every Christian who had reached the age of discretion to confess their sins at least once a year to their own parish priest and to receive the Eucharist at least at Easter. Historians observe, however, that this canon did not invent the practice, but confirmed earlier legislation and customs.

The council met in the Lateran Basilica of Saint John, in Rome, beginning on November 11, 1215, with one of the largest episcopal assemblies in history: about 404 bishops, in addition to 71 patriarchs and metropolitans and 800 abbots and priors. It was at this same council that the Church formulated the doctrine of transubstantiation, which gives the Eucharistic precept a particular doctrinal weight. Thus, the third precept is not a mere annual formality, but the minimal expression of the union of the faithful with "the Body and Blood of the Lord", the center of sacramental life.

itens.titulo: Observe the Days of Fasting and Abstinence
itens.resumo: Fourth precept of the Church: to keep the appointed times of penance, such as Lent, especially Ash Wednesday and Good Friday.
itens.corpo: The fourth precept asks the faithful to observe the days of asceticism and penance established by the Church, above all the days of fasting and abstinence from meat set in the calendar — in current practice, mainly Ash Wednesday and Good Friday — as a spiritual preparation and a concrete act of penance.

itens.titulo: Providing for the Needs of the Church
itens.resumo: Fifth precept of the Church: to contribute, according to one's own means, to the material support of the Church.
itens.corpo: The fifth precept reminds us that the Church, even though she is above all a spiritual community, needs material resources to sustain her worship, her clergy, and her works of charity and evangelization, and it asks each of the faithful to contribute to this according to his or her means — a duty distinct from, yet complementary to, general charity toward the poor.

itens.resumo: The twofold commandment of love of God and neighbor, which Jesus presents as the synthesis and key to reading the entire Decalogue.
itens.corpo:
Asked which was the greatest commandment of the Law, Jesus answered by citing two texts of the Old Testament: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind" (Deut 6:5) — the first and greatest commandment — and "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Lev 19:18), "like it." And he concluded: "On these two commandments depend all the law and the prophets" (Mt 22:37-40).

The Catechism teaches that it is in the light of this twofold and single commandment of charity that the whole Decalogue must be interpreted: the first three commandments refer chiefly to the love of God, and the remaining seven, to the love of neighbor (CCC 2052-2055). This does not relativize the concrete commandments, but reveals their unity and their ultimate purpose — which Saint Paul confirms when he writes that "he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law" (Rom 13:8-10).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2052-2055

itens.resumo: The teaching that the Ten Commandments form an indivisible whole: to gravely transgress even one is, in a certain way, to compromise the whole Law.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches that the Decalogue forms an indivisible whole: each "word" refers to each of the others and to all of them; they reciprocally condition one another, and the two tablets of the Law illuminate one another, constituting an organic unity (CCC 2069). To transgress one commandment is, in this sense, to infringe the whole Law, an idea the Apostle James already expressed: "For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it" (Jas 2:10).

This unity has an important practical implication: it is not possible to choose to keep only the commandments considered more convenient or less demanding. The coherence of the Decalogue reflects the oneness of God himself, who revealed it, and of the one love — of God and of neighbor — that the whole Law expresses.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 2069

itens.titulo: The Decalogue and the Natural Law
itens.resumo: The teaching that the Ten Commandments, although revealed by God to Moses, make explicit a moral law already inscribed in the conscience of every human being.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches that the Ten Commandments state the essential requirements of the natural law (CCC 2070): even someone who has never heard of biblical revelation can, in principle, recognize through reason a good part of their content — as Saint Paul observes about the Gentiles, who "do by nature what the law requires", showing "the work of the law written on their hearts" (Rom 2:14-15).

If a good part of the Decalogue is therefore accessible to reason, why did God need to reveal it? The Catechism itself answers: humanity, wounded by sin, has difficulty knowing with certainty and without admixture of error the requirements of the natural law; for this reason, in the history of salvation, a positive and supernatural revelation was necessary to confirm and make explicit these requirements (CCC 2071).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2070-2071

itens.titulo: The New Law and the Fulfillment of the Decalogue
itens.resumo: The teaching that Christ, in the Sermon on the Mount, did not abolish the Ten Commandments but brought them to their fullness, revealing even deeper demands of the heart.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism presents the "New Law" or "Law of the Gospel" as the perfection on earth of the divine law, natural and revealed — the work of Christ, expressed above all in the Sermon on the Mount (CCC 1965-1968). Jesus himself says: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill" (Mt 5:17), and then he deepens the meaning of specific commandments — for example, teaching that whoever looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Mt 5:27-28).

This fullness is not a relativization of the commandments, but an interior radicalization: the New Law is not content with the correct external act, but asks for the conversion of the heart itself, and finds its ultimate synthesis in the "new commandment" that Jesus leaves to the disciples on the eve of the Passion: "Love one another as I have loved you" (Jn 13:34).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1965-1974
